title: Weeks 5-6 of building an Elder Scrolls game set in Black Marsh: process of building out a lore-consistent set of ~600 game locations
author: Potential_Ad_7544
selftext:
This project is about making a childhood dream come true - making an Elder Scrolls game set in Black Marsh/Argonia. I've always loved the lore and the feel around that part of the elder scrolls universe. And simultaneously, none of the releases that have come out since Morrowind really scratch the same itch that game did, in terms of its depth, oddity, and sense of mystery.

So the goal with this project is to develop a standalone mod/spin-off, with the scale of a full Elder Scrolls game, set in Black Marsh, properly grounded in elder scrolls lore, that feels like Morrowind but with more modern gameplay.

(for context, I code professionally - I run a team of data scientists/ML engineers, and have been using AI coding for work in various guises for at least 4 years now - but have no game dev experience).

The last few weeks I've been working with Fable & Opus on building out a set of places that are varied but consistent, fully grounded in the province's lore (and logical extrapolations from it). I've been going through a human-in-the-loop process on \~20 places so far, with the goal of building up an agent skill that can then run unattended to roll out the full set of \~580. There are just 3 small ones in the video, plus some examples from the (unpolished) combat sandbox; this is me going through one of the iterations of checking the agents' output. 

My feeling is that it's pretty easy to have an agent throw down a bunch of buildings for a demo scene, or do some procedural generation to create a big world. But what I want is a big world (size of Skyrim's map) which is as **densely filled** as a game like Morrowind, and where everything in it **feels** hand designed and non-generic and real. This feels like an interesting challenge and the sort of thing that AI struggles with if you're trying to go down more of the one-shot route.

This ended up being pretty involved. I'm interested to know if anyone else is doing anything similar and what lessons you've learned so far?

# Process so far

(Fable lead orchestrator, fanning out various subagents for different types of tasks).

**Foundations and lore**

\- Set the era first: 4E 201, about same time as Skyrim. Empire no longer rules here.

\- Swept UESP wiki to pull canon lore / info. Worked out what gaps we have for our era.

\- Filled each gap by projecting/logically deriving from canon. Always aiming for the least inventive answer that works. Idea was to extrapolate from known canon out to a reasonable state that the province could plausibly be in by 4E 201 - who rules, what factions are there, what are the major cities like, what sorts of places would you expect to find in the world, etc.



**Land**

\- Started with [All Tamriel Heightmap](https://www.nexusmods.com/skyrimspecialedition/mods/573) as a coarse prior. Argonia in this game is approximately Skyrim's in-game map size.

\- Pinned canonical map coordinates for the known cities.

\- Defined eight culture zones + ecological region types, each changing movement, visibility, building style, materials, sound and threats. Inferred reasonable cultural zones from the known and extrapolated lore, and on mined fan theories and ideas from reddit & other online forums from older TES games.

\- Rough shape extrapolated from lore: colonised edges, unconquered heart. Imperial infrastructure visibly decaying inward — surveyed, adapted, flooded, abandoned.

\- Generated the actual 3D terrain across the whole province, and a World Studio app to inspect it in. Then did a second pass on scale, mountain relief and naturalness. Judged on foot in character mode, tweaked and refined over multiple rounds of feedback.

\- Solved rivers, lakes, hydrology and drainage. Much of the province is swamp, so more granular decisions on what places go where need to be shaped by the water system.

\- Built out the rest of the world stuff from [the last update](https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/s/dvXehjhxNV) (weather, calendar, lighting, vegetation etc etc)



**Quests and narrative**

\- We can't have a fully finalised set of places before we've decided what our story will be, what side quests we'll have, what the faction questlines will be; but also can't have all of our quests set before we know what places will be available for them to happen in. So there was a two-way process between authoring story and quests and authoring places.

\- Agent research on Morrowind quest density and distribution across province. And on what people most liked and disliked about questlines from Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim.

\- Sketched out the main quest via rounds of iteration between me and Fable. Partially inspired by agent summaries of research on fanfic ideas for stories set in Black Marsh from fan forums (credited in the repo). Landed on a plotline where you play as a prisoner who has been recorded dead, are recruited as an agent for a faction whose powerbase is teetering, and undertake a province-wide treasure hunt to stop a powerful death-cult from destroying or enslaving the province - or turn double agent and join them.

\- Similarly authored lore-grounded faction questlines and wide set of varied but coherent potential minor quests.

\- Extensive back and forth between place requirements and quest requirements, defining what the world must physically provide — interiors, routes, underwater volumes, evidence sockets, NPC home/work spots, alternate stealth/swim/climb approaches.

\- Named characters and creature checked against assets we can actually deliver.

\- Lots and lots of work on making any player-facing prose not sound like it's AI-written crap. Work in progress. Rounds of agent research online into what the giveaways are for "AI written" (there is some good academic research on this), plus many rounds of me manually reading and feeding back on player-facing prose. Written into a rulebook and an automated reviewer agent that checks all prose against it.



All of this before we even start putting anything in the world (!)



**Places**

\- Three levels of siting: 1) macro, 2) meso, 3) micro

\- Macro - what exists, and roughly where. Wrote out a roster of potential places on our 'menu' to plot. Cities, villages, camps, shrines, ruins, farms, docks, wrecks, etc. Something like 700 in total. For each one, I had agents write a causal record - why does this exist? Why is it here? What is the point of it for the player? etc etc. Grounded in the lore, hydrology, culture zone, trade routes, story, quests etc. Then had Fable develop a solver to plot all the places on a 2d map, following a set of rules and preferences developed by a combination of me + Fable (I also had it set subagents to do research on good open-world RPG game design to look for principles to follow, and specific games liek Morrowind and BOTW etc). Solver places them all at once, honouring what each record promises, checking spacing so the province doesn't clump or grid up. 

\- Meso — siting each place on the actual ground. The macro layer places by landform class. The meso pass goes and measures the real terrain and moves the place to where it can stand - e.g. A dock isn't a dot on a map in reality, it's a set of buildings on a coast next to water deep enough for a boat - so for waterside places the berth is chosen first and the settlement is hung off the bank above it. 

\- Micro — the buildings themselves. Each place gets a blueprint: which building kit, which parcels, which structures, laid out to the rules for that culture and settlement type. Lots of iteration with Fable on this, puting together building kits. e.g. Making kits only combine pieces that were designed to combine — no jamming a stilt house onto a stone arch because the descriptions sound compatible. Design everything for flood cycle: stilts, boardwalks, upper-floor life, ferry access, flooded quarters as a feature.

\- Agent checks object by object in the blueprint to see if all the nice prose we wrote about each place (e.g. the promises it makes about what it will provide to the player's experience) gets delivered at the micro level. If the record says a place is a "service hub", something checks that the blueprint contains shop, inns, smiths, etc. 

\- The **finally** the actual placement of buildings. Doing a small number of exemplar places first, with a view to hand-holding and tweaking initially, to develop a set of rules and principles that an agent can then use to roll out all the other places without me having to painfully feed back on every one (hopefully...)



.....Then after doing a few iterations on the exemplars, discovered we'd introduced a horrible circular dependency where placing settlements led to tweaks to the landscape (e.g. raising or lowering bits of land so buildings had room to sit) which automatically triggered water to re-sve which invalidated some placements (e.g. places authored as "riverside" had their water moved away), and at the same time water placement seemed to be getting buggier and buggier. Went round in that loop a bunch of times for finally concluding we needed to rearchitect and try a different approach...



So went \*all the way back\*, had another couple of Fable agents review the whole process and plan, rewrite it to address everything, then go back through all the phases again.



... \*Then\* discovered a bunch of performance/framerate issues (including somehow having introduced a thing where 50,000 trees were being drawn one at a time every frame) and spent a couple of days going back and forth fixing and optimising those...



Then rethought the place building loop a few times and spent a while replanning it (needs to be able to scale to efficiently build 580 places unsupervised), so turned the approach more into something where we build a set of agent Skills, iteratively through testing on a small number of places, and make it self improving and self checking so it can eventually be scaled out. Taking into account consistency with the quest system, lore, future NPC system to be built, interiors, etc.

**Where it is now**

Have 20 smallish places built across 10 different types (villages, camps, dungeons, temples, underwater argonian type places, that sort of thing) and a blueprint created for the first big city. All of these places have 'sockets' (feel like that's a claude word) placed for things like NPCs, quest markers, items, containers etc that will then get filled in by later phases. You can see these in a bit of the video (that's so I can check if it looks like the placement rules are putting them in sensible places).

I'm aiming to 'de-risk' by building slices of each system to a point where I'm confident they'll work, then will do a full automated roll out later on. So when an agent can build one of each of the 10 types of place and a full city perfectly first time, I'll rule that as good to go, then move onto the next system (next one planned is swimming, climbing and boats). Think we're a way off that yet.

comments.author: RUSuper
comments.body:
While I can respect the dedication I do wonder if using Elder Scrolls IP is really a good idea, if it gets attention you are really shooting yourself in the foot here, maybe switch direction towards random RPG with it's own story. 

Just a thought here.

replies.author: Potential_Ad_7544
replies.body: Appreciate the thought! My thinking here is that I'm intending it more as part of the modding scene, rather than as a totally new game. Kind of more like a standalone open source Skyrim mod. (Tbh with hindsight I probably should've just made it as an \*actual\* mod using whatever people use for AI-assisted modding in the actual engine. I started off doing it as a standalone open world as an experiment and kind of got too far into that to easily switch!) Not intending for it to be commercial, if that makes any difference, but may be an issue anyway

replies.author: Potential_Ad_7544
replies.body: A bit like this project: [https://beyondskyrim.org/project/argonia](https://beyondskyrim.org/project/argonia) (theirs will be vastly better than mine as they've got a whole team of people who are much more skilled than I am; I kind of just wanted to see how far I could get developing my own version as that one still seems to be a way off any releases)

replies.author: Sleisl
replies.body: There's precedence for other TES mod projects that have vastly increased the game world or added new areas/continents. I think if they aren't commercializing it and they don't happen to run over exactly what Bethesda are doing with TES6, they shouldn't have much to worry about.

replies.author: karl_mainz
replies.body: Best to make it similar to, yet legally distinct from, The Elder Scrolls tbh

comments.author: eejdoowad
comments.body: Wow, i really like the approach you've taken of defining data, constraints, solvers, and using those to generate the world. That's a lot of data. How are you organizing it?

comments.author: inr222
comments.body: Hey, this is awesome, thanks for sharing

comments.author: toothpastespiders
comments.body:
I'm seriously impressed. I actually forgot the AI generated nature of the environments a few times during the video as I got distracted by considering the thematic elements on their own merits. 

There's a lot of really nice flavor elements that I think are really well done, like the mounted head on a wall. I always really appreciate that kind of thing in games. Where you can learn about a culture by extrapolating. Whether it's seeing patterns in clouds or intentional design is less relevant in my opinion when it comes to overall immersion. Obviously the latter is better but the former can still draw me in. 

I've actually been hoping someone would try out a project like this so I'm really glad I stumbled onto your post! The fleshing out of an untouched region is an especially fun point I think. But there's also just something inherently interesting about having AI do full world building. 

My projects are generally more focussed on internal states and ecosystems. So very detailed at a very small scale with larger elements lazily modeled from ecologies in the real world. But that curiosity about how a system might be able to expand the world for me always comes up. Even apart from playing it as a game, there's just something really fun about the concept of exploring a world created like that. 

Mostly though, huge props to you on your architecture and methodology. It seems like a really well thought out foundation to build on.
